title: The plague of Cyprian
hookLine: when plague came, letters from two bishops describe Christians staying to nurse the sick, their own and others

lines: I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.
A CITY WHERE DISEASE IS SPREADING.
cards: "I was sick, and ye visited me." That's Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, describing the day the nations are gathered and sorted. The people who visited the sick are startled: when did we see you sick?
And the answer: when you did it for the least of these, you did it for me. It's an easy line to admire on a calm day.
It's a different line in a city where a disease is spreading, nobody knows how, and the sick are dying in their houses and streets.
Two bishops, Cyprian in Carthage and Dionysius in Alexandria, lived through days like that, and their words survive.

teach.b: Dionysius first. In a letter the historian Eusebius preserved, he describes what the Christians of Alexandria did in the plague, or most of them, he says. In paraphrase: out of great love, they didn't spare themselves.
They clung to one another, visited the sick without fear and cared for them, and some who nursed others caught the disease and died, taking their neighbors' sickness on themselves.
Others in the city, he says, pushed the sick away and fled, even from those dearest to them. That's one bishop's proud account of his own people.
But the picture is specific: hands that wash and feed, and a cost that's paid. In Carthage, Cyprian's deacon Pontius wrote his bishop's life.

When the plague came, he says, Cyprian taught his people that it isn't remarkable to care only for your own. If you want to be children of the Father, do good to everyone, even those who persecute you.

teach.h: THE RICH GAVE MONEY, THE POOR LABOR.
teach.b: Then he set them to work by what they had: the rich gave money, the poor their labor. Cyprian also wrote a short book, On Mortality, for frightened Christians who were dying too, and asking why.
He doesn't pretend the plague spares them.

teach.h: THE PLAGUE SHOWS WHAT'S IN PEOPLE.
teach.b: He says it shows what's in people: whether the healthy care for the sick, whether families truly love each other, whether doctors stay with their patients. Not a statistic, and not a claim that only Christians were brave.
Writing from two cities, saying one plain thing about their people. They stayed.

how: Christians count visiting the sick among the works of love in Matthew 25, and some churches organize hospital visits, meals and prayers for people who are ill.

games.q: you're Cyprian. plague is in the city, and your people ask who they should help first. what do you say?
o: our own people first. we can't help everyone.
everyone, even the people who persecute us.
nobody. stay inside and stay safe.
games.why: Pontius says he taught them to do good to all, not only their own, and set each to work by what they had.

practice: Let one face come: someone sick right now, in a hospital, in bed at home, or worn down by something long and quiet that others have stopped asking about.
Think what would actually help, a message, soup, a ride, an hour of sitting with them; Cyprian's rule fits here: give what you have. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Cyprian. The bishop of Carthage in whose days a plague struck, when writers in two cities said Christians nursed the sick, their own and others, even at the cost of their lives.

orig.note: Latin: on mortality. the title of Cyprian's short book for Christians frightened by the plague.

carryVoice: Your line: they stayed. Two cities, two bishops, and one plain thing to say. Be well.
